§YStratocratic Conservatism§! follows the idea that a strong figure from the military can ensure stability within the country and is essential to maintaining national unity and safeguarding tradition, placing strong emphasis on the nation, religion and monarchy.

A stratocratic conservative government differs from a military junta or an outright dictatorship in that democratic institutions are retained to legitimize authority and maintain public participation, but they are still skewed to serve the government

SIA_rama_x_char_desc.value:
General Prayut Chan-o-cha, commonly known as "Big Tu", was born into a military family, a background that led him into a career in the armed forces. He became well known within the 21st Infantry Regiment of the King's Guard as the "Queen's Tiger", a reputation that contributed to his rise to Commander-in-Chief of the Royal Thai Army in 2010, a position he had long aspired to attain.

During the political turmoil of 2014, marked by deep divisions and prolonged unrest, Prayut led the military under the National Council for Peace and Order (NCPO) in a coup on 22 May 2014, aiming to end the political crisis. This action resulted in his appointment as Prime Minister.

As Prime Minister, Prayut oversaw the drafting of a new constitution focused on national unity and anti-corruption, earning it the nickname "the anti-corruption constitution", though several provisions—such as allowing a non-MP to become Prime Minister and empowering the Senate—were controversial.

After the 2019 general election, Prayut returned to office with the support of the Palang Pracharath Party, promoting policies to assist low-income citizens, reduce living costs, and address agricultural issues. Despite continued criticism from younger and left-wing groups over the constitution and his rule, he retained strong support from conservative groups as a stabilizing leader.

SIA_country_summary.value:
§YCountry Summary§!:
Thailand, the “Land of Smiles,” is renowned for its culture, cuisine, and tropical beauty. But behind this globally admired image, persistent structural problems that have shaped the country`s modern history. Since the 1932 transition to a constitutional monarchy, Thailand has endured repeated cycles of political upheaval, alternating between military rule and civilian government. From World War II and the Cold War to the aftermath of the 1997 Asian financial crisis the nation has faced various instability and political upheaval 
These tensions have intensified since the 2014 coup, with Thailand remaining under General Prayut Chan-o-cha even after the official dissolution of the military junta. Political polarization has deepened, with many becoming increasingly disillusioned with the junta-backed establishment. 
The new decade will be a challenge for the Thai people. Will they break the cycle and progress toward a brighter future? Only time will tell.

SIA_lack_of_the_political_legitimacy_des.value:
£GFX_SIA_prayut_coa_cat





Thailand`s political legitimacy has been repeatedly questioned due to the unelected Senate, which plays a decisive role in selecting the Prime Minister and influencing governance despite lacking democratic representation. This has created a widespread perception that the Senate serves as a safeguard for certain political groups rather than the public interest. Likewise, the Election Commission has been criticized for alleged bias and lack of transparency, with accusations of manipulating electoral processes to favor particular parties. These factors have significantly eroded public trust in elections as a true reflection of the people’s will.

The slim majority in the House of Representatives further weakens the government`s stability, forcing it to engage in behind-the-scenes bargaining with smaller parties or independents. This dependency on undemocratic mechanisms—along with the influence of appointed institutions—reinforces the view that political power in Thailand is disconnected from genuine democratic choice. Consequently, public confidence in the legitimacy of the political system continues to deteriorate.

SIA_an_army_with_a_country_1_desc.value:
£GFX_SIA_army_with_nation_cat





The Royal Thai Army is regarded as the nation`s protective shield and a pillar of internal security. Despite facing challenges in adapting to modern warfare, the army continues to rely on traditional strategies and weaponry supported by foreign allies. Training remains rigorous, with an emphasis on discipline over tactical flexibility, resulting in a strong defensive capability but limited expertise in contemporary maneuver warfare. The army also maintains significant influence over national politics and governance, often ensuring that strategic decisions reflect its own interests.

Although the Royal Thai Army possesses well-prepared personnel and a stable organizational structure, its reliance on imported weapons and technological limitations prevent it from achieving full effectiveness in modern combat. A centralized command structure and the prioritization of internal power dynamics have hindered the development of long-term strategic planning. Nevertheless, its expertise in domestic operations and its ability to maintain internal order continue to make the Royal Thai Army a force that cannot be underestimated in Southeast Asia.

The Constitution of the Kingdom of Thailand (2017), the Highest law of the land have been proclaimed as the Constitution on the 6th of April 2017. However, the Process of the drafting of the Constitution have been controversial ever since. In, 2015 the Constitutional Drafting Committee submitted their Draft of the Constitution into the National Reform assembly, Of which the draft failed to passed. Extended the Length of the NCPO. Before in 2016 the New Constitutional Drafting Committee lead by Meechai Ruchuphan's draft passed the National Reform Steering Assembly and then passed the nationwide referendum.

The Controversies around the Constitution included, the "Temporary" 250-Military appointed Senators and their exclusive power to voted on the Prime Ministerial Nomination during their time as Senators, The "Special" requirement of the Constitutional Amendment that the Majority of the National Assembly shall included 1/3 of the Senators and the "Independent Organizations" which were subjected and appointed by the Senators.

SIA_parliament_detail_pprp_desc.value: §YPalang Pracharath Party§! is a Thai political party founded in 2018 to support the continuation of General Prayut Chan-o-cha`s government following the planned 2019 elections. Widely regarded as the political arm of the military establishment, the party drew its core support from conservative voters, the military, and business elites.\n\nThe party`s core platform focuses on §Ynational stability, economic development under strong leadership, and continuity§! of the policies enacted under the NCPO. Despite criticism for its close ties to the junta, Palang Pracharath emerged as the largest party in the 2019 election by popular vote, forming a coalition government that returned Prayut to the premiership.

SIA_parliament_detail_ptp_desc.value: §YPheu Thai Party§! is a Thai political party founded in 2008 following the dissolution of the People Power Party, with the aim of continuing the political ideology and mass support base of the Thai Rak Thai Party.\n\nThe party`s core platform focuses on §Yreducing social inequality, stimulating economic growth, and improving the quality of life§! for the general public. Pheu Thai has played a major role in Thai politics, having formed governments on several occasions, and has been led by prominent political figures such as §YThaksin Shinawatra§! and §YYingluck Shinawatra§!, making it one of the most influential political parties in contemporary Thailand.

SIA_parliament_detail_ffp_desc.value: §YFuture Forward Party§! is a Thai political party founded in 2018 by billionaire auto-parts heir Thanathorn Juangroongruangkit. The party quickly gained massive support among younger Thais and progressives, campaigning on §Ydemocratic reform, anti-military intervention in politics, decentralization, and economic modernization§!.\n\nIn the 2019 election, the FFP won 53 seats, making it the third-largest party. However, the party faced constant legal challenges and was ultimately dissolved by the Constitutional Court in February 2020, with its executives banned from politics for 10 years.

SIA_parliament_detail_dp_desc.value: §YDemocrat Party§! is Thailand`s oldest political party, founded in 1946. Traditionally representing the urban middle class, professionals, and southern Thai voters, the party has long positioned itself as a champion of §Yconstitutionalism, rule of law, and liberal democratic values§!.\n\nDespite its historical prominence, the party`s influence has waned in recent elections. In 2019, it joined the Palang Pracharath-led government coalition, a controversial decision that cost it support among its progressive base.

SIA_parliament_detail_bjt_desc.value: §YBhumjaithai Party§! is a Thai political party founded in 2008. Under the leadership of Anutin Charnvirakul, the party has carved out a niche focusing on §Ypragmatic populism, rural development, and public health reform§!.\n\nNotably, Bhumjaithai became the first party in Thailand to champion the legalization of cannabis for medical and economic purposes. The party joined the government coalition after the 2019 election, securing key cabinet positions including the Ministry of Public Health.

SIA_parliament_detail_tlp_desc.value: §YThai Liberal Party§! is a minor Thai political party led by former national police chief Sereepisuth Temeeyaves. The party positions itself as a §Yliberal, reformist party§! advocating for police reform, anti-corruption measures, and civil liberties.\n\nIn the 2019 election, the party won 10 seats and aligned with the opposition bloc.

SIA_parliament_detail_ctpp_name.value: £GFX_chartthaipattana §YChart Thai Pattana Party§! (Phak Chart Thai Pattana)

SIA_parliament_detail_ctpp_desc.value: §YChart Thai Pattana Party§! is a Thai political party that emerged from the dissolution of the original Chart Thai Party. Led by the Silpa-archa political family, the party maintains a §Yconservative, business-oriented platform§! with strong support in central Thailand.\n\nThe party joined the government coalition after the 2019 election, contributing 10 seats to the ruling majority.

SIA_parliament_detail_pcc_desc.value: §YPrachachat Party§! is a Thai political party founded in 2018, primarily representing the §YMuslim-majority provinces in southern Thailand§!. Led by veteran politician Wan Muhamad Noor Matha, the party focuses on issues affecting the Deep South, including §Ypeace and reconciliation, cultural rights, decentralization, and economic development§! in the border provinces.\n\nIn the 2019 election, the party won 7 seats, all from southern constituencies, and aligned with the opposition.
